name: Intuitive eating

lead: Intuitive eating, created by dietitians Evelyn Tribole and Elyse Resch, replaces diet rules with attention to hunger, fullness and satisfaction. People use it to cut diet stress and bingeing and to settle into a stable weight and better body satisfaction.

Its ten principles include rejecting the diet mentality, honouring hunger and fullness, making peace with food and coping with emotions without food. Their book Intuitive Eating was first published in 1995. Reviews link it with better psychological outcomes, while evidence on long-term weight and physical health is limited or mixed.

paras: People stop counting and restricting, eat when hungry and stop when comfortably full, and allow all foods. It is common in eating disorder recovery and body image circles, often with guidance from a dietitian. It is a change in approach built up over months rather than a short programme.
It is not a weight-loss method, and long-term weight data are limited. Some medical conditions need structured diets, and the lack of concrete rules can make it hard to apply.

chain: Eat by hunger and fullness cues
angle.text: Intuitive eating swaps diet rules for hunger and fullness cues, aiming for less diet stress and bingeing and a steadier weight and body satisfaction. It has good psychological correlates; evidence on weight change is weaker.

lead: Intuitive eating is an approach to eating that centres on the body's hunger and satisfaction cues rather than external diet rules, with the stated aim of building a positive relationship with food instead of controlling weight [1]. It was coined by registered dietitians Evelyn Tribole and Elyse Resch, whose book Intuitive Eating was first published in 1995 [2]. For people interested in appearance, its appeal is in the chain it describes: less restrict-and-binge cycling and food preoccupation can mean steadier eating, a more settled body image and more energy for training, sleep and skincare habits that shape how someone looks day to day [1][3].

Its ten principles include rejecting the diet mentality, honouring hunger and fullness, making peace with food, challenging the 'food police' and coping with emotions without food [1][2]. Research links it with better psychological outcomes such as higher body appreciation and lower disordered eating, while evidence on weight and physical health is mixed or limited [3][4][5]. Intuitive eating is not designed as a weight-loss programme, and it is often discussed alongside the Health at Every Size movement [1][6].
infobox: Evelyn Tribole and Elyse Resch (registered dietitians)

paras: The framework rejects chronic dieting and moral labelling of foods, and emphasises permission to eat, attention to hunger and satiety, satisfaction, respecting the body and gentle movement [1][2]. It is not designed as a weight-loss method [1].

The ten principles, as listed by Wikipedia, are: reject the diet mentality; honour your hunger; make peace with food; challenge the food police; feel your fullness; discover the satisfaction factor; cope with your emotions without using food; respect your body; exercise; and honour your health [1]. Unlike most diets it bans or restricts no specific foods and treats foods as neither good nor bad [1].

Researchers have proposed an acceptance model of intuitive eating, in which feeling accepted by others helps people appreciate their bodies and resist viewing themselves from an observer's perspective, which in turn supports eating intuitively; the model has been tested in women across emerging, early and middle adulthood [7]. Studies have also linked intuitive eating with interoceptive sensitivity, the ability to perceive internal bodily signals [8].

Tribole and Resch developed the approach from clinical work with chronic dieters in the early 1990s, and their book appeared in 1995 with later editions in 2000, 2012 and 2020, according to Grokipedia (an AI-generated source) [2]. Wikipedia notes the term first appeared in a 1990s peer-reviewed article, and that the 2012 edition, subtitled A Revolutionary Program that Works, set out ten components and reviewed the related research [1]. Tylka published the Intuitive Eating Scale in 2006 and the revised IES-2 in 2013, which added positively worded items and an extra component of intuitive eating [9]. An Intuitive Eating Scale-3 was reported in 2024 [10].

sections.h: Use for appearance and body image
paras: Within body image and eating disorder recovery communities, intuitive eating is described as a way to leave dieting behind without pursuing a particular body size. Wikipedia reports links with self-esteem, self-compassion, body appreciation and quality of life, and says it may reduce weight stigma and dieting [1]. A 2021 meta-analysis of 97 studies, 89 percent of them cross-sectional, found intuitive eating inversely associated with eating pathology, body image disturbance and psychopathology (correlations from -.23 to -.58) and positively associated with positive body image and self-esteem [3]. A longitudinal analysis of the EAT 2010-2018 cohort reported that intuitive eating predicted better psychological health and lower use of disordered eating behaviours [11].

On T Nation, lifters occasionally discuss eating by feel. One poster argued that if intuitive eating produced a large calorie surplus it might mean the person was usually under-eating, while others report mixed experiences and a return to tracking [12][13].

A six-month randomised trial of 78 obese female chronic dieters compared a health-at-every-size programme that included intuitive eating with dieting and followed participants for two years [6]. A 2014 literature review of 26 articles (17 cross-sectional, 9 clinical studies of which 8 were randomised) found intuitive eating negatively associated with BMI and positively associated with psychological health indicators, and concluded that clinical studies showed weight maintenance but perhaps not weight loss [4]. A 2014 review examined interventions promoting eating by internal cues [14].

A 2017 structured review of 68 publications found mindfulness-based approaches most effective for binge and emotional eating, and described the evidence base for intuitive eating as limited at that time [5]. A 2021 meta-analysis of psychological correlates is described above [3]. A 2021 systematic review of randomised trials of mindful or intuitive eating interventions examined effects on dietary intake [15]. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine intervention studies reported a large pooled improvement on the Intuitive Eating Scale (1.50) and positive changes on other health outcomes [16]. A 2026 randomised trial compared a mindfulness-based programme with education grounded in intuitive eating principles in adults with overweight or obesity [17]. Wikipedia summarises findings as associations with higher self-esteem and body appreciation, possible improvement in cholesterol, glucose and blood pressure, and limited evidence on long-term weight [1].

Researchers cited by Wikipedia say evidence on long-term weight outcomes is insufficient, that results vary between people, that some medical conditions may require prescribed diets, and that the lack of concrete food rules can make it hard to apply; Wikipedia also categorises the topic under pseudoscience, reflecting disputes about its evidence [1]. Observational links with lower BMI may reflect reverse causation [1]. Most correlational research is cross-sectional, which limits conclusions about cause [3]. Grokipedia notes ongoing debate over its suitability as a standalone obesity strategy without complementary nutrition guidance [2].
The approach is discussed in eating disorder recovery and body image communities. Wikipedia says it may reduce eating disorder symptoms but that evidence is still developing [1].
